newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel and PLO resume talks prodded by Clinton.
newsitem.headline: Israel and PLO resume talks prodded by Clinton.

text.p: Israel and the Palestinians resumed talks on a self-rule accord for the town of Hebron, prodded by U.S. President Bill Clinton who insisted the time had come for a deal.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat spoke by phone on Sunday and their negotiators met on Monday, ending a 10-day break marked by shootings and tensions over Jewish settlements.

"I'm pleased that the prime minister and Chairman Arafat talked yesterday. That's a good thing, better than not talking. But sooner or later they have to do something," Clinton said at the White House in his toughest language to date on the subject.

"They've had an agreement within grasp with very little difference on Hebron for some time now. The time has come to make that agreement," Clinton, who has made Middle East peace a cornerstone of his foreign policy, told reporters.

Since a White House summit prompted by bloodshed nearly three months ago, Israel and the PLO have failed to agree on security arrangements which Netanyahu wants to protect some 400 Jews in the heart of Hebron, amid more than 100,000 Arabs.
On Monday evening Yitzhak Molcho, an adviser to Netanyahu, met Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat in Jerusalem on Hebron. A PLO official said they would resume talks on Wednesday.
Under a 1995 deal signed in Washington by Arafat and then-Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, Israel is supposed to hand over 80 percent of Hebron to Palestinian rule.

Rabin, a Nobel peace laureate, was assassinated in November 1995. Netanyahu, the right-wing Likud party leader, was elected in May this year vowing to guard Israeli security following a wave of suicide bombings that killed 59 people in Israel.

Israeli-PLO tensions flared in the last week over Israel's decision to grant financial benefits to Jewish settlers, the killing of a settler mother and her son by Arab gunmen, and the fatal shooting of an Arab worker by a Jewish farmer.
A White House spokesman said on Monday that Washington found the latest Israeli policy on settlements "a complicating factor" in efforts to reach peace.
Clinton, asked if he would call West Bank settlements an obstacle to peace, told reporters: "Absolutely".

James Baker, Secretary of State under Clinton's predecessor George Bush, was the last senior U.S. official to apply the "obstacle to peace" terminology to settlements. Israel's relations with its U.S. ally reached a 35-year low over a Likud-led settlement boom at the time.
President Bush held up $10 billion in loan guarantees over the issue, awarding them only after Rabin came to power in 1992 by ousting Likud and freezing new settlement.

Netanyahu lifted the freeze after taking office this year. About 130,000 Jews live in the settlements scattered among two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.

In a letter addressed to Netanyahu and made public by his office on Monday, three former secretaries of state including Baker and five other former U.S. officials urged Israel to refrain from expanding Jewish settlements.
"We are concerned that unilateral actions, such as the expansion of settlements, would be strongly counterproductive to the goal of a negotiated solution," the letter said.
